name: Yoruba tribal marks

lead: Yoruba tribal marks, called ila in Yoruba, are patterns of scars cut into the face, usually in infancy, that show family lineage, subgroup and place of origin. They are also described as a form of beauty and adornment within the culture.

They are a body-modification tradition rather than a modern cosmetic method. Interest in looksmaxxing and body-modification circles comes from its status as a permanent facial alteration with deep cultural meaning, though its use has declined sharply since the late twentieth century.

paras: Traditionally a specialist cut patterns such as horizontal, vertical or triangular lines on the cheeks, temples or forehead and rubbed in substances such as charcoal to produce raised scars. Patterns differed by lineage and region; examples named in one reference include three parallel horizontal lines linked to Oyo subgroups.

Scarification with unsterile tools carries infection risk, including bloodborne infections when tools are shared, and can produce keloid scars. Nigeria has restricted non-medical scarification of minors, and the marks have been associated with social stigma in urban employment.

angle.text: The marks directly alter the face's appearance and were regarded within the culture as both an identity marker and an aesthetic. They are a traditional rather than a modern cosmetic technique, and their use has been falling.

lead: Yoruba tribal marks, known as ila, are deliberate scarification patterns made on the face and sometimes the body of Yoruba people of southwestern Nigeria, Benin and Togo. They denote lineage, subclan, geographic origin and, according to descriptions of the tradition, aesthetic enhancement.[1]

Scarification in general is the permanent marking of skin by cutting, scratching or branding; healing takes roughly six to twelve months, and scars are often made raised by packing wounds with substances such as clay or ash.[2] Facial marks like these are therefore a permanent appearance change made in childhood and carried for life.

Yoruba oral tradition, as summarised in Grokipedia, traces the marks to the mythic ancestor Oduduwa and describes their role in identifying kin during conflicts and the slave trade. This account is oral-historical and AI-compiled rather than established archaeological fact, though terracotta heads from Ile-Ife show line markings.[1]

paras: Marks are cut as horizontal, vertical or triangular configurations on the cheeks, temples and forehead. Different patterns indicate lineage or origin; pele, three parallel horizontal lines, is linked to Oyo subgroups, and gobiri, clustered vertical lines, to Borgu influences.[1]

Yoruba tradition attributes the practice to Oduduwa, who is said to have marked his children's faces so they could be identified if scattered by war. Terracotta heads from Ile-Ife dated to about 1200-1400 CE show vertical line marks, which Grokipedia presents as evidence of pre-colonial entrenchment.[1]

The marks are also described as signalling status, offering spiritual protection, and, in some beliefs about abiku children, deterring early death.[1] Scarification more broadly serves as a rite of passage, an identity marker and in some cultures a perceived medical measure.[2]

Traditionally an itinerant specialist known as an oloola made the cuts, often with razors or blacksmith-made tools, and rubbed in charcoal or similar material to promote keloid scarring. Herbal applications followed, and outcomes varied with the practitioner's skill and hygiene.[1]

Descriptions attribute the decline to colonial-era missionary condemnation, Nigerian legal restrictions on non-medical scarification of minors, urbanisation and stigma around employment. Debate pits cultural preservation against child welfare concerns such as infection and irreversible marking.[1] Scarification overall has been stigmatised or criminalised by colonial governments and missionaries, and in some cases continued as resistance.[2]
Infection is common when tools are not sterilised, and shared tools have been linked to the spread of HIV and hepatitis C. Substances used to encourage keloids can lead to unwanted keloid scars.[2]
